2. The plaintiff instituted the suit for establishment of title and confirmation of possession or in the alternative for recovery of khas possession in the suit land and for a declaration that the order made in Vested Property case in respect of the suit land was illegal. His case was that the suit land measuring 3.15 acres appertaining to CS khatian No. 749 of Karaitala Mitha mouza along with other lands originally belonged to one Rahimuddin and Rupsan Bibi in moiety share. Rupsan died leaving her 2 daughter, Sabera Khatun and Tulson Bibi. Sabera died having husband Gahar Ali, daughter Chand Banu and sister Fulson. Chand Banu died unmarried leaving father Gahar Ali who subsequently married Fulson after the death of her first husband. Fulson also died leaving son Afezuddin, 2 daughters Aiful (through her first husband) and Lal Banu, Aiful inherited 18 gandas and 3 karas share in the property and sold the same to Kinu Bhuson, benamder of Rajendra Chandra Das and Khirod Chandra Das Rahimuddin also sold his -/8/ annas share to the said Kinu Bhuson on 6th Baishak, 1335 BS, benamidar of the said Rajendra and Khirod. Thereafter Rahimuddin, Reazuddin and Gaisuddin took settlement of the said land from Rajendra and Khirod on the 7th Baishak, 1335 BS by executing a fraudulent Kibuliat in the name of Kinu Bhuson and subsequently surrendered the said land by a deed of relinquishment (Istafanama) dated 10th Jaistha. 1344 BS and on the same date they took settelment of 1.43 and 1.82 acres of land from CS Khatian No. 745 and 741 respectively from the landlord by executing a kabuliat and got the land recorded in their names in GS khatian No. 745 and 741. The rest 1.18 acres of land of CS. khatian No. 745 and total 2.66 acres of CS khatian No 749 remained with the landlord as his khas land. Rahimuddin and his son Reazuddin by executing borga kabuliats used to cultivate the said land on yearly basis under the landlord. The 7 annes 1 ganda 11 kara share in the CS khatian Nos. 745 and 749 of Gahar Ali, Afezuddin and Laibaru devolved ultimately upon Dud Moher Bibi and Sharaf Ali who sold the same on 17th Chaitra 1347 BS by registered kabala to Kaisaruddin beramdar of the plaintiff No. 1. The plaintiff subsequently also took settlement of 1.18 acres and 2.66 acres of land from CS khatian No. 745 and CS khatian No. 749 respectively on 5th Baishak 1361 BS in the benami of Kaisaruddin from the said Rajendra and Khirod. As the land of C S khatian No. 742 & 749 was recorded wrongly in the names of Rajendra and Khirod the plaintiff filed P.S. No 201 of 1956 through his benamidar Kaisaruddin against Khirod and heirs of Rajandra and got a compromise decree on 17.5.36 and recorded his name under section 54 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Kaisaruddin executed a deed of relinquishment in respect of land of CS Khatian No. 749 in favour of plaintiff No. 1. The plaintiff No. 1 sold 1. 22 acres to plaintiff No. 2 from CS Khatian No. 749 (SA 902) on 6-8-68. and 1.72 acres to Dr Anwar Hossain on 13-4-64. Subsequently Fazlul Karim and others purchased the said land from Dr Anwar Hossain who sold the right of reconveyance of defendant No. 2 who redeemed the land. The suit land was auction sold in certificate case No. 1784/68-69 and the plaintiffs got the auction sale set-aside through his benamder Kaisaruddin, Kinu Bhusan also executed 'Muktipatra' in favour of Rajendra on 14-4-64. The proceeding In the MR, Case No. 562 of 1970 brought by the plaintiff over the suit land was illegally dropped and defendants being encouraged made an attempt to disturb continued possession in the suit land. Hence this suit. 

 3. The defendant Nos. 1, 4, 5, 8, 9(ka) to 9(gha) predecessor of defendant Nos. 9, 11 and 12 contended the suit by filing separate written statement. The suit was decreed by the learned Munsif. But on appeal it was remanded to the trial court. However, after remand defendant No. 1 alone contested the suit by the filing a written statement and an additional written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable it was barred by limitation and was bad for defect of parties. His case was that Kinu Bhusan was the original and real owner of 12.05 acres of land of CS Khatian Nos. 741, 749, 745 and 751. Rahimuddin, Reazuddin and Gaizuddin took settlement of the entire 12.50 acres of land from Kinu Bhusan by registered Kabuliat dated 7th Baisakh, 1335 BS corresponding to 25-4-28 at a rental of Rs 175/- 13 annas 6 pies and were in possession of the same by constructing their homestead etc. and by cultivating. His further case was that on the death of Gaizuddin 1/3rd share in said kabuliant land devolved upon his father Rahimuddin and mother Moiful Bibi. Subsequently who sold the same to one Kashem Ali on 17th Chaitra 1374 BS corresponding to 31-3-41. Kashem Ali also sold that land to the defendant No.1 and others Reazuddin died leaving 2/3rd share which was inherited by his son defendant No. 1, widow Moiful and Bibi daughter Pabonjan. Pabonjan also died leaving mother Mouful Bibi and brother defendant No. 1 and husband Sultan Howlader. Thus the defendant No. 1 had been possessing the suit land. Defendant No.1 also denied the story of surrender of the kabuliat land by Rahimuddin and others by Istafanama in favour of the land lord Rajendra and Khirod and the story of subsequent settlement from the landlord by Rahimuddin and others. The story of barga cultivation under Rajendra and Khirod or their benamder Kinu Bhusan was also denied by the defendant No. 1. He further case was that was plaintiff No. 1 obtained the decree in Title Suit No. 201 of 1956 fraudulently and collusively the decree was not binding on him as he was not a party in the suit. He also contended that Money Suit No. 6 of 1969 instituted by Nur Hossain, brother of the plaintiff No. 2 was dismissed and the appeal taken therefrom was also dismissed. His further case was that the Criminal proceedings brought by the plaintiffs in respect of the suit land was also dismissed and his possession was established in all criminal proceedings in respect of the suit land. 

 6. In support of his contention he also referred me to the case of Gendla Bepari vs Abdul Mansur Mia and ors, reported in 19 DLR 349. This is also a decision of a single Bench of this Dhaka High Court. In that case the question of admissibility of a certified copy of a plaint also came up before the Bench for consideration. His Lordship Abdullah, J on interpretation of the provision of section 74 of the Evidence Act held that plaint or a written statement on being admitted and registered after presentation in the record of the Court comes within the definition of sub-section (1) section 74 of the Evidence Act. In that case it was also held that when a plaint is presented and Court passes an order admitting or registering the plaint as well as the order are entered into the record and they form a part of the record. The learned judge observed:— 

 7. In this respect it may be mentioned that after pronouncement of judgment in the case of Tarkeswar Prasnd Tewari vs Devendra Prasad Tewari which was considered in PLD 1967 (Lah) 1951 a full Bench of Madras High Court had an occasion to deal with this question in the case of Katikineni Venkata Gopal Naras-simha vs Chitluri Venkataramayya reported in 1940 (Mad) 768 wherein it has been held that both plaint bad written statement are public documents. I have gone through the decision reported in PLD 1967 (Lah) 1051 as well as 19 DLR 349. I prefer to follow the view taken by his Lordship Abdullah, J which I consider to be a correct exposition on the interpretation of section 74 of the Evidence Act. The plaint of a suit, in my opinion, as soon as it is registered by the Court on presentation it forms part of the record of the judicial officer within the meaning of clause (in) of sub-section (1) of section 74 of the Evidence Act and as soon as it forms part of the records of judicial officer it becomes admissible in evidence. In this view of the matter, with the reference to the learned judge who decided the case reported in PLD 1967 (Lah) 1057 I am unable to follow the view taken by him. Therefore the contention of the learned Advocate that the finding of the Lower Appellate Court is based on inadmissible evidence viz the certified copy of plaint of TS No. 201 of 1956 cannot be upheld. The learned Advocate for the petitioners also submitted that the finding of the lower appellate court regarding 'Estafa' by the tenant Rahimuddin, Reazuddin and Gaizuddin in favour of the superior landlords was also not based on proper consideration of evidence as the learned Appellate Court did not advert to the reasoning of the trial court and consider evidence relied on by it. The learned Advocate for the opposite, parties, on the other bands, submitted that in this case although the Lower Appellate Court did not consider all the documents on record which were considered by the trial court yet the finding being based on sufficient evidence cannot be interfered with by this court. I was taken through the judgments of the both courts, From the judgment of the lower appellate court it appears that it took into consideration the averments made in the plaint of Title Suit No. 201 of 1956, miscellaneous proceeding case No 562 of 1970 and Money Suit No. 6 of 1969 for the purpose of holding that the surrender was not acted upon. The finding as to whether a document by which certain land was surrendered was acted upon or not has to be arrived at with reference to the evidence on record. Although the lower Appellate Court did not take into consideration each and every piece of document considered by trial Court in arriving at the finding regarding surrender of the land by Rahimuddin, Reazuddin and Gaisuddin but then the Low Appellate Court on consideration of the certified copy of the plaint, Miscellaneous proceeding case and the Money Suit found that the deed of surrender was not acted upon. In this respect it is pertinent to observe that the Lower Appellate Court for arriving at a conclusion of its own on facts need not refer to each, and every piece of document considered by the trial court if the evidence relied upon by it for such conclusion are sufficient for arriving at such a finding either of reversal or affirmance. In this case learned Lower Appellate Court having based his finding on consideration of the aforesaid documents and evidence on record I do not think that the finding is liable to be set-aside.
